To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the noise in noisy telephone speech can be tracked using linear dynamical system (LDS) models with autoregressive predictors of order 1, and (b) the use of such predictors in a speech compensation algorithm leads to a significant gain in recognition performance.

(1) linear dynamical systems models can track speech noise, (2) the use of such systems to estimate the noise can significantly improve speech recognition performance, and (3) the use of predictors of order greater then 1 does not significantly improve performance over the use of a predictor of order 1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of linear dynamical system noise models in speech processing.
the following questions: 1) What is the best order of autoregressive predictor to use for tracking the noise process?
the use of linear dynamical system modeling of the noise process for noise tracking.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a linear dynamically modeled noise process for tracking the noise process in a speech signal is a very effective approach to improving speech recognition performance.
the use of higher order autoregressive predictors for noise tracking is not justified, and the use of first order autoregressive noise models is adequate.
the use of higher order autoregressive predictors for tracking noise does not improve recognition performance beyond that obtained using a first-order predictor and, hence, is not justified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the first-order autoregressive predictor is the best model for tracking the noise.
first-order autoregressive predictors provide a simple and efficient way of tracking noise for speech enhancement and recognition.
a first-order predictor is sufficient to track the noise in noisy signals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a first-order predictor is all that is necessary to track noise.
, for the problem of tracking noise, a first-order model is sufficient and is computationally efficient.
